newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ex-Elf chairman targeted in payments probe.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Elf chairman targeted in payments probe.

text.p: The former chairman of French oil firm Elf Aquitaine has been targeted in an ongoing probe of suspect commissions paid in Elf's 1992 purchase of a former East German refinery, justice sources said on Thursday.

Loik Le Floch-Prigent, who chaired the state-owned oil giant from 1989 until 1993, has been formally placed under investigation on suspicion of ordering the payment of 13.5 million marks ($7.8 million) to an intermediary in connection with the purchase of the Leuna refinery, the sources said.
Investigating judge Laurence Vichnievsky suspects the former executive of misappropriation of company funds, they said.

Le Floch-Prigent has previously been placed under investigation in several other arms of the probe, which initially focussed on alleged financial irregularities at Elf and has since branched out to cover suspicious commission payments in Germany, Gabon and Venezuela.
The Leuna plant was acquired from the Treuhandanstalt, an agency of the German government in charge of privatising the former communist state's industries.

French media have reported that a total of more than $50 million in secret commissions allegedly were paid by Elf in connection with the transaction, funnelled through Swiss bank accounts and shell corporations.
However, Swiss and French investigators examining the purchase have so far been unable to trace the payments to their ultimate recipients.
In particular, the probes have turned up no proof that any of the money found its way into the coffers of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democratic Union, according to the media reports.
The CDU has flatly denied reports that it took bribes in connection with the deal, and the Paris public prosecutor's office said in April that it had no evidence of covert payments.
Elf has consistently declined comment on the probe.
